text: Hello (peace be upon you). peace be upon you. The universal opener. Say it first, say it to elders, say it even if you were just in the room two minutes ago. Greetings: You can give and return a proper salaam
Hello back (and peace upon you). and upon you, peace. The reply. Skipping it is how you end up as a topic at the next family dinner. Greetings: You can give and return a proper salaam
Hi (a quick salaam). The short version, for cousins and people your own age. Greetings: You can give and return a proper salaam

Yes / respectful 'sir, ma'am'. Stick ji on anything to make it polite: Khala ji, ji haan, ji shukriya. Your new best friend. 'Ji' means yes, and also turns anything respectful: Khala ji, Abbu ji. Greetings: You can give and return a proper salaam
How are you? (respectful, to a man). To a man you respect. 'Aap' is the polite you; 'hain' goes with it. Greetings: You can ask an elder how they are and answer when they ask you
How are you? (respectful, to a woman). To a woman. Only one sound changes: kaise → kaisi. Greetings: You can ask an elder how they are and answer when they ask you
How's it going?. what condition is?. Works for everyone, any gender. The safe option when your brain freezes. Greetings: You can ask an elder how they are and answer when they ask you
I'm fine. 'Theek' = fine, okay. You'll say it 40 times a day. Greetings: You can ask an elder how they are and answer when they ask you

Thank God (= I'm well). praise be to God. The default answer to 'how are you' in most Pakistani homes. What most people actually answer. It means you're fine without you having to commit to any details. Greetings: You can ask an elder how they are and answer when they ask you
Everything's fine
And you? (respectful). Always bounce the question back. It's just manners. Greetings: You can ask an elder how they are and answer when they ask you
Thank you. Thank you. You'll need it: someone is about to hand you chai. Greetings: You can give and return a proper salaam
you (respectful). Elders, strangers, in-laws, teachers, your friend's parents. The verb ends in 'hain'. Greetings: You can pick aap, tum or tu for the person in front of you
you (casual). Friends, cousins your age, younger siblings. The verb ends in 'ho'. Greetings: You can pick aap, tum or tu for the person in front of you
you (intimate, or rude). Best friends, small children, God, and people you are yelling at in traffic. The verb ends in 'hai'. Greetings: You can pick aap, tum or tu for the person in front of you
I
How are you? (casual, to a guy). Same question, casual. Notice aap…hain became tum…ho. Greetings: You can pick aap, tum or tu for the person in front of you
How are you? (casual, to a girl)
How are you? (intimate, to a guy)
Yes (polite). Polite yes. Just 'ji' works too, and is what you'll mumble most. Greetings: You can say yes, no, thank you and sorry politely
No (polite). Polite no. Will not actually stop anyone putting more rice on your plate. Greetings: You can say yes, no, thank you and sorry politely
Yeah
No / not
Thank you very much. 'Bohat' = very, a lot. Add it to anything. Greetings: You can say yes, no, thank you and sorry politely

Thanks, that's kind of you. kindness. Works as 'thank you' and, with a request, as 'please'. A warmer, more old-school thank-you. Aunties love it. Greetings: You can say yes, no, thank you and sorry politely
Sorry / excuse me (respectful). please forgive. Sorry or excuse me. For stepping on feet and interrupting gossip. Greetings: You can say yes, no, thank you and sorry politely
No problem / never mind. it's no matter. The gracious reply to an apology. Greetings: You can say yes, no, thank you and sorry politely

Okay / good / oh really?. The Swiss Army knife of Urdu. Tone does all the work. Achha. (Okay.) Achha? (Really?) Achhaaa. (I see.) ACHHA. (Enough.) One word, infinite meanings. Greetings: You can say yes, no, thank you and sorry politely
What's your name? (respectful). 'Aap ka' = your (respectful). Naam = name. Easy one. Greetings: You can introduce yourself and your parents
My name is Ali. 'Mera' = my. Swap in your own name. The verb goes last: my name Ali is. Greetings: You can introduce yourself and your parents
Nice to meet you. having met you, happiness happened. Long, but it makes aunties melt. Worth the effort. Greetings: You can introduce yourself and your parents
Who is this? (respectful). 'Yeh' = this, 'kaun' = who. 'Hain' because you're being respectful about them. Greetings: You can introduce yourself and your parents
This is my mum. 'Meri' for a woman…. Greetings: You can introduce yourself and your parents
This is my dad. …and 'mere' for a man you respect. Yes, 'my' changes too. Urdu is thorough. Greetings: You can introduce yourself and your parents

dear / kiddo (literally 'son'). Elders call every younger person beta, girls included. You are 'beta' until you are about 50. Means 'son', but elders say it to everyone younger. A stranger aunty calling you beta is normal. Enjoy it. Greetings: You can introduce yourself and your parents
Goodbye. God be your protector. The classic goodbye. Greetings: You can say goodbye properly (and survive the long version)
Goodbye (the other common version). God be your protector. Just as common. Use whichever your family uses. Greetings: You can say goodbye properly (and survive the long version)
See you again. we'll meet again. 'Phir' = again. A warm way to close. Greetings: You can say goodbye properly (and survive the long version)
Take care of yourself (respectful). 'Khayal' = care, thought. The '-iye' ending makes it respectful. Greetings: You can say goodbye properly (and survive the long version)

Say salaam to your mum. Nobody leaves a Pakistani house without being handed a salaam to deliver. You will be given salaams to deliver. Delivering them is not optional. Greetings: You can say goodbye properly (and survive the long version)
Good night

God willing (= hopefully / we'll see). From a parent, 'Inshallah' can mean anything from 'definitely' to 'absolutely not'. Attach to any plan. 'Phir milenge, Inshallah.'. Greetings: You can say goodbye properly (and survive the long version)

Bless you (an elder's 'live long'). keep living. You'll hear this, not say it. The right reply is a small smile and lowered eyes. An elder's blessing as you leave. You don't say it back; you just glow. Greetings: You can say goodbye properly (and survive the long version)
Mum. Ammi, Ammi jaan, Mama, Mummy: families vary. Ammi is the classic. Family: You can name your closest family in Urdu
Dad. Abbu, Abba, Papa. Same man, same opinions about the thermostat. Family: You can name your closest family in Urdu
brother. Also what you call any man roughly your age. The waiter is bhai. The Uber driver is bhai. Brother. Also every man you need something from. Family: You can name your closest family in Urdu
sister. Sister. The 'h' is soft: beh-en. Family: You can name your closest family in Urdu
son. Son. (Yes, and also everyone under 50, as you learned.). Family: You can name your closest family in Urdu
daughter. Daughter. Same pattern: -a for him, -i for her. Family: You can name your closest family in Urdu
children / kids
Mum's father (maternal grandad). Mum's dad. Nana = mum's side; remember N for 'Nani's husband'. Family: You can name everyone on your mum's side
Mum's mother (maternal grandma). Mum's mum. Judge, jury, best halwa. Family: You can name everyone on your mum's side
Mum's sister (maternal aunt). Mum's sister. Shabnam Khala is one of these. Brace yourself. Family: You can name everyone on your mum's side
Khala's husband. Khala's husband. Usually quietly watching cricket. Family: You can name everyone on your mum's side
Mum's brother (maternal uncle). Mum's brother. Traditionally the one who spoils you. Family: You can name everyone on your mum's side
Mamoon's wife. Mamoon's wife. Many families say 'Mami'. Family: You can name everyone on your mum's side
Dad's father (paternal grandad). Dad's dad. D for Dad's side: Dada, Dadi. Family: You can name everyone on your dad's side, including older vs younger uncles
Dad's mother (paternal grandma). Dad's mum. Family: You can name everyone on your dad's side, including older vs younger uncles
Dad's younger brother. Dad's YOUNGER brother. Calling Taya 'Chacha' makes him younger, and he will not thank you. Family: You can name everyone on your dad's side, including older vs younger uncles
Chacha's wife. Chacha's wife. (And Tai is Taya's wife.). Family: You can name everyone on your dad's side, including older vs younger uncles
Dad's older brother. Dad's OLDER brother. Seniority is everything. Family: You can name everyone on your dad's side, including older vs younger uncles
Taya's wife
Dad's sister (paternal aunt). Dad's sister. In TV dramas, the villain. In real life, usually lovely. Usually. Family: You can name everyone on your dad's side, including older vs younger uncles
Phuppo's husband. Phuppo's husband. Family: You can name everyone on your dad's side, including older vs younger uncles
brother's wife (sister-in-law). Your brother's wife. Also what you call a friend's wife. Family: You can talk about cousins and in-laws (and survive 'are you married?')
in-laws (your spouse's family). Your spouse's family. Comes up a lot once you're married. Comes up even more before. Family: You can talk about cousins and in-laws (and survive 'are you married?')

cousin (yes, just 'cousin'). Urdu has proper terms like 'khala-zaad bhai' (khala's son), but every Pakistani family just says 'cousin'. Just 'cousin'. Everyone code-switches here, and that's real Urdu. Family: You can talk about cousins and in-laws (and survive 'are you married?')
family / clan
my (with a masculine noun). 'My' works the same way: mera (m), meri (f), mere (plural or respect). Family: You can say whose relative someone is (Ammi ki behen, Abbu ke bhai)
my (with a feminine noun). Family: You can say whose relative someone is (Ammi ki behen, Abbu ke bhai)
my (plural, or a respected man). Family: You can say whose relative someone is (Ammi ki behen, Abbu ke bhai)
big / older
small / younger
Mum's sister. Mum of sister. Behen is feminine → ki. And Ammi ki behen = Khala. Family: You can say whose relative someone is (Ammi ki behen, Abbu ke bhai)
Dad's sister. Same shape. Abbu ki behen = Phuppo. Family: You can say whose relative someone is (Ammi ki behen, Abbu ke bhai)
Mum's brother. An uncle is a respected man → ke. Ammi ke bhai = Mamoon. Family: You can say whose relative someone is (Ammi ki behen, Abbu ke bhai)
Dad's older brother
Dad's younger brother
Nani's house. Ghar (house) is masculine → ka. Family: You can say whose relative someone is (Ammi ki behen, Abbu ke bhai)
This is my aunt (mum's sister)
This is my uncle (mum's brother)
This is my brother
This is my sister
I have two brothers. my two brothers are. Urdu doesn't 'have' siblings: it says 'my two brothers are'. Family: You can introduce your family and say how many siblings you have
I have one sister. my one sister is. One sister → hai (singular). Two brothers → hain. Family: You can introduce your family and say how many siblings you have
How many brothers and sisters do you have?. 'Bhai behen' together = siblings. Family: You can introduce your family and say how many siblings you have
How many children do you have?
Who is that? (respectful). Point (discreetly) at someone at the dawat. Family: You can introduce your family and say how many siblings you have
Bilal is my cousin. Family: You can talk about cousins and in-laws (and survive 'are you married?')
He's a doctor. You will hear this sentence about Bilal more than you hear your own name. Hear it once, hear it forever. Family: You can talk about cousins and in-laws (and survive 'are you married?')
My family is very big. Bara = big. Every Pakistani khandan is bohat bara. Family: You can introduce your family and say how many siblings you have
What's your mum's name?
Are you married?. The question. Asked at every gathering, by every aunty. Family: You can talk about cousins and in-laws (and survive 'are you married?')
Not yet. not now. The answer. Add 'Aunty' and a polite smile. Family: You can talk about cousins and in-laws (and survive 'are you married?')

Whose son are you?. The classic elder question. They're placing you on the family map. Elders place you by your parents. Answer with your dad's (or mum's) name: “Main Shahid ka beta hoon”. Family: You can introduce your family and say how many siblings you have
Food's on the table. food has been laid. The call to the table. Drop everything. Nobody waits. Dawat Survival: You can name the food on a desi table
In the name of God (said before eating). Said quietly before the first bite. Dawat Survival: You can name the food on a desi table
flatbread. Dawat Survival: You can name the food on a desi table
rice. Dawat Survival: You can name the food on a desi table
curry. The generic word for any curry with gravy. Any curry. 'Aaj kya salan hai?' = What curry is it today?. Dawat Survival: You can name the food on a desi table
lentils. Dawat Survival: You can name the food on a desi table
meat. Dawat Survival: You can name the food on a desi table
vegetables / veg curry. Dawat Survival: You can name the food on a desi table
sweets. Dessert. There is always room. Dawat Survival: You can keep up with a host's running commentary
tea
water
sugar
chilli / spice heat. Heads up: 'thori si mirch' in a desi kitchen is not a little. Dawat Survival: You can say what you like and don't like to eat
It's delicious. Mazedaar = tasty. The bare minimum. Dawat Survival: You can praise the food and the cook properly
The food is really good. Dawat Survival: You can praise the food and the cook properly
The tea is really good
That was amazing!. enjoyment came. Casual and enthusiastic: 'That was amazing!'. Dawat Survival: You can praise the food and the cook properly

You cook so well. there's great flavour in your hands. The ultimate compliment to the cook. Say this to Nani and you're in the will. The power move. Elders will repeat it to everyone. Dawat Survival: You can praise the food and the cook properly
Enough, enough!. Say it with a hand over your plate. Words alone do not stop a desi host. Dawat Survival: You can stop a host refilling your plate (eventually)
I'm full. my stomach has filled. Dawat Survival: You can stop a host refilling your plate (eventually)
No more, thank you. Dawat Survival: You can stop a host refilling your plate (eventually)
just a little. The tactical compromise. Accept a little, stop a lot. Dawat Survival: You can stop a host refilling your plate (eventually)
Have some more, dear. You'll hear this every 90 seconds. Dawat Survival: You can stop a host refilling your plate (eventually)
I'd like some tea. to me, tea is needed
I'd like some water
Could I have some water?. will water be got?. Softer than 'chahiye'. Perfect with elders. Dawat Survival: You can ask for tea, water, and less sugar
Will you have some tea? (respectful). Never a real question. The chai is already brewing. Dawat Survival: You can ask for tea, water, and less sugar
Yes, of course. Dawat Survival: You can ask for tea, water, and less sugar
Less sugar. Say this immediately. Desi chai default sweetness is 'dentist's retirement fund'. Dawat Survival: You can ask for tea, water, and less sugar
I like biryani. to me, biryani is liked
I don't like spicy food
What's this?. Dawat Survival: You can say what you like and don't like to eat
Who made this?. Ask this, then praise whoever made it. Dawat Survival: You can praise the food and the cook properly
piping hot. 'Fresh roti, garam garam!' Accept it. Resistance is futile. Dawat Survival: You can keep up with a host's running commentary
The food's getting cold. Every host's battle cry. Means 'stop talking and eat'. Dawat Survival: You can keep up with a host's running commentary

You shouldn't have gone to the trouble!. why did you take trouble?. The guest's ritual line when a lavish spread appears. The host will say 'koi takleef nahin'. Dawat Survival: You can praise the food and the cook properly
No trouble at all. Dawat Survival: You can praise the food and the cook properly
Hello? Can you hear me?. is the voice coming?. The opening line of every international call since 1987. Phone Calls: You can handle a bad phone line in Urdu
I can't hear you. the voice isn't coming. Phone Calls: You can handle a bad phone line in Urdu
The line's bad. Code-switch alert: 'line' is English, and everyone says it. Phone Calls: You can handle a bad phone line in Urdu
You're breaking up. your voice is cutting. Phone Calls: You can handle a bad phone line in Urdu
Speak louder, please. speak with force. Respectful '-iye' ending. To a cousin: 'zor se bolo'. Phone Calls: You can handle a bad phone line in Urdu
Say that again, please. Phone Calls: You can handle a bad phone line in Urdu
I'll call back later (said by a man). A man says 'karta hoon'…. Phone Calls: You can wrap up a family call and promise to call back
I'll call back later (said by a woman). …a woman says 'karti hoon'. Phone Calls: You can wrap up a family call and promise to call back
Send a voice note, please. Pakistan's national communication format. Minimum length: four minutes. Phone Calls: You can wrap up a family call and promise to call back
Who's speaking?. Phone Calls: You can say who's calling and ask kya, kab, kahan, kaun, kyun, kaise
It's Ali speaking. Men say 'raha'…. Phone Calls: You can say who's calling and ask kya, kab, kahan, kaun, kyun, kaise
It's Sara speaking. …women say 'rahi'. The verb tells everyone your gender. Phone Calls: You can say who's calling and ask kya, kab, kahan, kaun, kyun, kaise
what?
when?
where?
who?
why?
how?
Where are you?. Phone Calls: You can say where you are and what you're doing
I'm at home. Phone Calls: You can say where you are and what you're doing
I'm at work. Phone Calls: You can say where you are and what you're doing
What are you doing?. With aap, it's always 'rahe hain'. Phone Calls: You can say where you are and what you're doing
I'm cooking
I'm cooking
I'm studying. Parhna = to study / read. Every parent's favourite verb. Phone Calls: You can say where you are and what you're doing
I'm studying
When are you coming?. Asked on every call. 'Inshallah' is a valid answer. Phone Calls: You can wrap up a family call and promise to call back
What time is it there?. Asked at the start of every call. Answered wrong every time. Phone Calls: You can chat about time and weather across continents
It's night here. Yahan = here, wahan = there. Phone Calls: You can chat about time and weather across continents
How's the weather there?. Phone Calls: You can chat about time and weather across continents
It's really cold here. Phone Calls: You can chat about time and weather across continents
It's really hot there. Phone Calls: You can chat about time and weather across continents
How is everyone?. Phone Calls: You can wrap up a family call and promise to call back
Salaam to everyone. Mandatory. Calls cannot legally end without it. Phone Calls: You can wrap up a family call and promise to call back
We miss you. Very common code-switch. The formal 'yaad aa rahi hai' is next to it. The way most people actually say it. Phone Calls: You can chat about time and weather across continents
I miss you so much. your memory is coming a lot. The lovely, proper way. Phone Calls: You can chat about time and weather across continents

3 o'clock. baje = o'clock. Teen baje = 3:00. Numbers, Time & Money: You can tell and ask the time, including half and quarter past
half past three. saare = and a half. Saare teen = 3½ = 3:30. Numbers, Time & Money: You can tell and ask the time, including half and quarter past
quarter past three. sawa = and a quarter. Numbers, Time & Money: You can tell and ask the time, including half and quarter past
quarter to four. paune = a quarter less than. Paune chaar = 3¾. Numbers, Time & Money: You can tell and ask the time, including half and quarter past

I'm 20. my age is twenty years. Swap in your own age. Numbers, Time & Money: You can talk about when things happen and say your age
today. Numbers, Time & Money: You can talk about when things happen and say your age

yesterday OR tomorrow. Same word. The verb tense tells you which. Yes, really. Kal = yesterday AND tomorrow. Context does the rest. Numbers, Time & Money: You can talk about when things happen and say your age
the day after tomorrow (or before yesterday). Numbers, Time & Money: You can talk about when things happen and say your age
morning. Numbers, Time & Money: You can talk about when things happen and say your age

In just five minutes. In desi time, this means 45 minutes. Plan accordingly. Numbers, Time & Money: You can talk about when things happen and say your age

Please sit. Getting Around: You can give polite commands and invitations

Go straight on. Getting Around: You can give and follow simple directions

Turn left. Baayen = left. They rhyme. Good luck. Getting Around: You can give and follow simple directions
Drive slowly, please!. Possibly the most-used phrase in any Pakistani rickshaw. Getting Around: You can give and follow simple directions
Where's the mosque?. Getting Around: You can ask where something is and understand the answer
Where's the bathroom?. Everyone in Pakistan says 'washroom'. Asking for the 'toilet' gets a wince. Getting Around: You can ask where something is and understand the answer
in the bazaar. Getting Around: You can ask where something is and understand the answer
near the house. Getting Around: You can ask where something is and understand the answer
in front of the shop. Getting Around: You can ask where something is and understand the answer
behind the mosque. Getting Around: You can ask where something is and understand the answer

That's way too much. Getting Around: You can negotiate a fare without being fleeced (much)
Two hundred is fair. Getting Around: You can negotiate a fare without being fleeced (much)
Final price?. Getting Around: You can negotiate a fare without being fleeced (much)
Forget it, then. The walk-away. Say it, turn around, walk slowly. Count to three. Getting Around: You can negotiate a fare without being fleeced (much)
Two teas, one samosa. Numbers come before the thing: do chai, ek samosa. Getting Around: You can order at a dhaba and ask for the bill
The bill, please. Casual code-switch. Everyone says bill. Getting Around: You can order at a dhaba and ask for the bill
wedding / marriage
henna night (the fun pre-wedding party). Weddings: You can name the events and people of a Pakistani wedding
the groom's procession (wedding day). Weddings: You can name the events and people of a Pakistani wedding
the reception, hosted by the groom's family. Weddings: You can name the events and people of a Pakistani wedding
groom. Weddings: You can name the events and people of a Pakistani wedding
bride. Weddings: You can name the events and people of a Pakistani wedding
drum night: singing, clapping, aunties' songs. Weddings: You can name the events and people of a Pakistani wedding
gift money (in an envelope). Cash in an envelope. The amount will be discussed by aunties for years. Weddings: You can name the events and people of a Pakistani wedding
Congratulations!. Works for weddings, babies, exam results, new cars. Weddings: You can congratulate the family and reply to congratulations
Happy wedding! (to the couple or family). Weddings: You can congratulate the family and reply to congratulations
Thank you (reply to mubarak). The automatic reply to any 'mubarak'. If someone says mubarak to you, this is the reply. Weddings: You can congratulate the family and reply to congratulations
I'll dance. Weddings: You can say what you will and won't do
I'll dance. Weddings: You can say what you will and won't do

When will the food be served?. Asked at every wedding at 11pm. Food is served at 1am. The question everyone is secretly asking. Weddings: You can survive 'you're next!' and 'when are you getting married?'
The bride looks beautiful. Say this. Mean it. It is always true at a wedding. Weddings: You can congratulate the family and reply to congratulations
You're next!. Said by every aunty to every single person at every wedding. Weddings: You can survive 'you're next!' and 'when are you getting married?'
God willing, soon. The diplomatic answer. Weddings: You can survive 'you're next!' and 'when are you getting married?'
When will you get married?. Future tense again: karoge = will you do. Weddings: You can survive 'you're next!' and 'when are you getting married?'
No idea / who knows. The honest answer. Weddings: You can survive 'you're next!' and 'when are you getting married?'
